raw_text:
Implantable cardioverter-defibrillators (ICDs) reduce sudden arrhythmic death in selected patients with prior ventricular arrhythmia or high-risk cardiomyopathy [1], [2]. Conventional transvenous ICDs are highly effective, but their intravascular leads create a lifelong substrate for fracture, insulation failure, venous obstruction, tricuspid valve interaction, endocarditis, and difficult extraction [3]. The subcutaneous ICD (S-ICD) was developed to preserve defibrillation efficacy while avoiding the vascular space and myocardium [4]. Its generator is placed laterally on the thorax and connected to a parasternal subcutaneous electrode; rhythm discrimination uses far-field electrograms rather than intracardiac signals.

Early human work showed that ventricular fibrillation could be reliably detected and terminated with a fully extrathoracic system [4]. Subsequent observational cohorts confirmed feasibility across different centres, operators, and patient groups [5], [6], [7], [8]. In the pivotal IDE study, acute conversion testing was successful in most patients and short-term freedom from device-related complications was high [9]. The EFFORTLESS registry and pooled IDE/EFFORTLESS analyses then provided larger, more pragmatic evidence: appropriate shocks were effective, lead-related intravascular complications were essentially eliminated, and most adverse events were pocket, wound, sensing, or generator related [10], [11], [12]. In a modern primary-prevention cohort using contemporary programming, the UNTOUCHED study demonstrated low inappropriate-shock rates while maintaining effective treatment of ventricular arrhythmias [13].

The strongest comparative evidence comes from PRAETORIAN, which randomized patients without pacing indications to S-ICD or transvenous ICD therapy. The S-ICD was non-inferior for a composite of device-related complications and inappropriate shocks, with fewer lead-related complications but more pocket-related events and no antitachycardia pacing (ATP) capability [14]. This trade-off defines clinical selection. The S-ICD is particularly attractive in younger patients, those with limited venous access, prior device infection, dialysis dependence, congenital heart disease, inherited arrhythmia syndromes, or anticipated long lead dwell time. It is less suitable when bradycardia pacing, cardiac resynchronization, or frequent monomorphic ventricular tachycardia likely to respond to ATP is expected.

Inappropriate therapy remains a central performance metric. Early S-ICD shocks were commonly caused by T-wave oversensing, myopotential noise, low-amplitude signals, or supraventricular tachycardia misclassification [15]. Pre-implant electrocardiographic screening therefore remains essential, especially in hypertrophic cardiomyopathy, Brugada syndrome, and congenital heart disease, where QRS/T-wave morphology can be dynamic [16]. Exercise or pharmacologic provocation may uncover rate-related sensing failure in selected patients. Implant position also matters: posterior generator placement, a left parasternal electrode close to the sternum, and avoidance of excessive fat between coil and thorax improve shock vector geometry. The PRAETORIAN score formalized radiographic assessment of implant position and predicts defibrillation-test failure risk [17].

Disease-specific experience is generally reassuring but nuanced. In hypertrophic cardiomyopathy, S-ICD therapy avoids transvenous leads in often young patients, but large T waves, QRS fragmentation, and exertional morphology shifts increase screening importance [18]. In Brugada syndrome, high right precordial ST-segment changes and fever- or drug-related repolarization shifts can affect sensing, yet multicentre experience supports use after careful screening [19]. Paediatric and congenital heart disease cohorts highlight the benefit of avoiding venous occlusion and intracardiac hardware, but smaller body size, growth, abnormal thoracic anatomy, and need for future pacing require individualized planning [20], [21].

Programming and device algorithms have improved outcomes. Dual-zone programming, higher conditional shock thresholds, morphology discrimination, and filters such as SMART Pass have reduced oversensing and inappropriate shocks [22]. Nevertheless, the S-ICD cannot deliver chronic pacing, ATP, or resynchronization. Defibrillation testing is still more commonly considered for S-ICD implantation than for contemporary transvenous ICDs, where randomized data showed that routine testing could often be omitted [23], [24]. In S-ICD practice, testing may be deferred in selected high-risk anaesthetic situations, but many operators still value it because shock vectors depend heavily on extrathoracic implant geometry.

Guidelines endorse the S-ICD for patients meeting ICD indications who do not require pacing, particularly when venous access or infection risk is a concern [25], [26]. Future directions include better sensing, smaller generators, longer battery life, standardized intermuscular implantation, remote monitoring, and combination with leadless pacing. Leadless pacemakers have proved the feasibility of intracardiac pacing without transvenous leads [27], and first clinical reports of combined leadless pacemaker/S-ICD systems suggest a modular pathway toward extravascular defibrillation plus pacing support [28]. Extravascular ICD systems placed substernally may eventually add ATP while avoiding transvenous leads, but long-term comparative data are still emerging [29]. Meta-analytic comparisons support the overarching message: the S-ICD is not a universal replacement for transvenous ICDs, but it is a mature, evidence-based alternative when defibrillation is needed and pacing is not [30].
